The proximal convoluted tubule is the part of nephron where majority of reabsorption occurs. Approximately 65–70% of filtered water is reabsorbed from the PCT into peritubular capillaries. choices.title: Metabolic alkalosis
choices.correct_explanation:
·         Excessive vomiting leads to depletion or removal of gastric HCL- leading to metabolic alkalosis associated with hypochloremia and hypokalemia. The excretion of a hydrogen ion leads to gain of a bicarbonate ion (HCO3-) in the extracellular space. HCO3− is then excreted by the kidneys as NaHCO3, resulting in volume depletion. The common causes of metabolic alkalosis are prolonged vomiting, hypovolemia, hypokalemia, etc. Hence, option d. is correct.

·         Respiratory acidosis occurs when there is hypoventilation resulting in accumulation of CO2 levels in the blood, which in turn lowers the pH. In this case, vomiting does not affect CO2 levels and hence, option a. is incorrect.

·         Respiratory alkalosis occurs when there is hyperventilation resulting in excessive loss of CO2, which raises the pH. In this case, vomiting does not affect CO2 levels. Hence, option b. is also incorrect.

·         Metabolic acidosis occurs when there is an excess acid or loss of bicarbonate, resulting in lowering pH. In this case, vomiting results in loss of stomach acid rather than bicarbonate. Hence, option c. is incorrect.

  • 45-year-old female with BMI 18 and has a sedentary lifestyle: A low BMI (18) suggests she is not overweight, which reduces the risk of type 2 diabetes, even with a sedentary lifestyle.

• The management of bleeding after administration of warfarin involves vitamin K, FFP (Fresh Frozen Plasma), etc. Anticoagulant should be put on hold and heparin should not be administered as it causes further bleeding. Hence, option a. is correct.
  • Vitamin K: Helps to reverse the effects of warfarin by promoting the synthesis of clotting factors.

choices.title: Addison’s disease
choices.correct_explanation:
• Sudden hypoglycemia occurs in Addison’s disease due to deficient counter-regulatory excretion of cortisol resulting in improved insulin sensitivity.
  • The patients with Cushing’s syndrome develop hyperglycemia due to hypercortisolism. The hypercortisolism blocks the action of insulin on peripheral tissues leading to increased insulin resistance. Hence, option c. is incorrect.
  • The patients with hypoparathyroidism develop hypocalcemia and hyperphosphatemia due to deficiency of parathyroid hormone. Hence, option d. is incorrect.
  • The patients with DM type II develop hyperglycemia rather than hypoglycemia. Hence, option b. is incorrect.

questions.title: Sudden hypoglycemia occurs in which of the following condition?

choices.title: Cushing syndrome
choices.correct_explanation:
• Excess glucocorticoids or hypercortisolism can cause hyperglycemia. The condition which affect the insulin action is known as Cushing syndrome. It is characterized by uncontrolled ACTH secretion leading to increase in cortisol production by the adrenal glands.
  • Addison Disease: Addison disease involves insufficient cortisol production, which usually leads to hypoglycemia (low blood sugar), not hyperglycemia.
  • Hyperparathyroidism: Hyperparathyroidism primarily affects calcium levels in the blood and does not typically cause hyperglycemia.
  • Hypoparathyroidism: Hypoparathyroidism involves low levels of parathyroid hormone and affects calcium levels, but it does not directly lead to hyperglycemia.

questions.title: <b>Hyperglycemia occurs due to which of the following disease condition?

choices.title: Cystourethrogram
choices.correct_explanation:
• A PUV is an obstructing membrane within the posterior urethra leading to partial or complete bladder outlet obstruction. A voiding Cystourethrogram and USG are used to investigate PUV.
  • Urethroscopy: Urethroscopy involves direct visualization of the urethra with a scope, which can also be used to diagnose PUV but is more invasive and not always the initial diagnostic test.
  • Ureteroscopy: Ureteroscopy is used to examine the ureters and kidneys, not the posterior urethra.
  • Sigmoidoscopy: Sigmoidoscopy is used to examine the sigmoid colon and rectum and is not relevant for diagnosing urethral conditions.

choices.title: Fat embolism
choices.correct_explanation:
• Fat embolism syndrome is associated with fracture of long bones, particularly femur. The fat cells in the bone marrow gain access to the venous sinusoids which have pro-inflammatory and pro-thrombotic potential.
  • Air Embolism: Air embolism is typically caused by the introduction of air into the venous system, often during invasive procedures or trauma, rather than a femoral fracture.
  • Pulmonary Embolism: Pulmonary embolism generally results from blood clots traveling from the deep veins (deep vein thrombosis) to the lungs, not from a femoral fracture.
  • Systemic Embolism: Systemic embolism refers to emboli traveling to various organs and tissues in the body, usually from the heart, rather than from a femoral fracture.

choices.title: Military TB
choices.correct_explanation:
• Hemoptysis is the expectoration of blood or blood-tinged sputum from the lungs. It is a common symptom in patients with pneumonia, TB, and sometimes in military TB. Miliary tuberculosis (TB) is a fatal form of disseminated disease due to the hematogenous spread of tubercle bacilli to the lungs and other organs. It results in the formation of millet seed-sized tuberculous foci. The clinical manifestations of acute military TB are dry cough with scanty sputum, dyspnea, and hemoptysis. Hence, option a. is correct.
  • Emphysema: Emphysema is characterized by the destruction of alveoli and air trapping but typically does not cause hemoptysis unless there is a co-existing condition such as chronic bronchitis or lung cancer.
  • Pneumothorax: Pneumothorax involves the presence of air in the pleural space and usually presents with chest pain and difficulty breathing, not hemoptysis.
  • Empyema: Empyema is the accumulation of pus in the pleural space, often secondary to pneumonia, but it does not commonly cause hemoptysis.

choices.title: Arsenic
choices.correct_explanation:
• The arsenic poisoning leads to the addition of the methyl group (CH3) to them by normal intestinal bacteria, which gives them the garlic-like odor. Hence, option c. is correct.
  • Arsenic poisoning is caused by the ingestion, absorption, or inhalation of dangerous amounts of arsenic.
  • Arsine is the simplest compound of arsenic and it is a colorless, flammable, non-irritating toxic odorless gas. When it gets oxidized by air, it produces a slight, garlic-like scent. Therefore, the people with arsenic poisoning have a garlic like odor.
  • Organophosphorus: Organophosphorus poisoning typically presents with symptoms related to the cholinergic system, such as excessive salivation, sweating, and muscle twitching, rather than a garlic-like taste.
  • Cyanide: Cyanide poisoning is associated with a bitter almond odor on the breath rather than a garlic-like taste.
  • Carbolic Acid: Carbolic acid (phenol) poisoning typically causes a burning sensation and the smell of the chemical itself, rather than a garlic-like taste.

choices.title: Altered mental status
choices.correct_explanation: • Charcot’s triad describes cholangitis as clinical findings of fever, right upper abdominal pain, and jaundice. The altered mental status is not included in the Charcot’s triad and hence, option d. is correct. However, the addition of shock and altered mental status is added by Reynolds pentad and is known as Reynold’s pentad.

The dysphagia to liquids and solids is present in the patients accompanied with regurgitation. Hence, option b. is correct.
  • Barrett Esophagus: Barrett Esophagus is a condition where the lining of the esophagus changes due to chronic acid reflux. While it can cause dysphagia, it typically affects solids first rather than liquids.
  • Esophageal Varices: Esophageal varices are dilated veins in the esophagus, often due to liver disease. They can cause bleeding but do not typically lead to early dysphagia for liquids.
  • Tonsillitis: Tonsillitis, an infection of the tonsils, can cause sore throat and difficulty swallowing but does not specifically lead to dysphagia for liquids first.

  • Sputum Test: A sputum test is used to diagnose respiratory infections and is not relevant for diagnosing typhoid fever.
  • Urine Routine: A routine urine test is not specific for diagnosing typhoid fever, although Salmonella Typhi may be present in urine later in the disease.
  • Stool Sample: A stool sample may be used to detect Salmonella Typhi in later stages of the disease, but it is not as reliable as a blood culture for early diagnosis.

choices.title: Tyramine rich diet
choices.correct_explanation: • MAOIs prevent the breakdown of tyramine found in the body and certain foods, drinks, and other medications. Patients taking MAOIs who consume tyramine-containing foods or drinks will exhibit elevated serum tyramine levels. A high level of tyramine can cause a sudden increase in blood pressure, called the tyramine pressor response. Examples of foods with high levels of tyramine include fish and certain meats, such as sausage, turkey, liver, and salami. Additionally, certain fruits can contain tyramine, such as overripe fruits, avocados, bananas, raisins, or figs. Further examples include cheeses, alcohol, and fava beans.

choices.correct_explanation:
• MAOIs can trigger a hypertensive crisis if patients consume foods or beverages high in tyramine or are exposed to specific pharmacologic agents. MAOIs can potentially cause drug-to-drug interactions, drug-food interaction, and overdoses, of which the patient should be aware. For example, patients should not be mixing MAOIs with other antidepressants like selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs). Combining these two drugs can cause serotonin syndrome, which is potentially fatal.
  • MAOIs prevent the breakdown of tyramine found in the body and in certain foods, drinks, and other medications. Patients that take MAOIs and consume tyramine-containing foods or drinks will exhibit high serum tyramine level. A high level of tyramine can cause a sudden increase in blood pressure, called the tyramine pressor response. Even though it is rare, a high tyramine level can trigger a cerebral hemorrhage, which can even result in death.
  • Examples of high levels of tyramine in food are types of fish and types of meat, including sausage, turkey, liver, and salami. Also, certain fruits can contain tyramine, like overripe fruits, avocados, bananas, raisins, or figs.

choices.title: Remove the old dressing by using sterile gloves
Clean the wound from center to periphery
choices.correct_explanation:
• The nurse should first use a clean pair of gloves to remove the old dressing and the after removing the dressing the nurse should discard the dressing into the yellow biomedical waste bin. After that the first priority is to inspect the wound for any discharge and foul smell, if not then the nurse should clean the wound from center to periphery using sterile dressing. Once the cleaning part is done, if the doctor has advised any ointment or spray that can be used otherwise then cover the wound with a sterile gauze pad which can be further supported by sterile dry cotton pad and secure the entire dressing with an adhesive.
  • Remove the old dressing by using sterile gloves: The old dressing should be removed using clean (non-sterile) gloves. Sterile gloves are typically used after the wound is exposed and ready for cleansing or when applying the new dressing.
  • Place a saline-soaked pad on the wound: A saline-soaked pad may be used for specific wound care protocols, but not universally. It depends on the type of wound and the dressing being used. Not all wounds require a saline-soaked pad.
  • Apply outer dressing directly over the wound: The outer dressing should be applied over an appropriate primary dressing that is in direct contact with the wound, which could be a sterile gauze, hydrocolloid, or another type of wound care material. The outer dressing is meant to secure the primary dressing, not to be in direct contact with the wound itself.

questions.title: The doctor ordered to administer 75 mL/hour 0.9% NS IV to a patient who just had a ‘CVP Line’ inserted through subclavian vein. The nurse started the infusion, and suddenly the patient felt agitated and shortness of breath. What would be the priority nursing action?

choices.title: Apply indirect pressure over the pressure points
Elevation of the affected limb above the heart level
choices.correct_explanation:
• The correct answer is elevation of the affected limb above the heart level.
  • The most effective general measure to be applied in case of active bleeding is application of direct pressure over the bleeding site.
  • The nurse may also raise or elevate the bleeding part of the body above the level of heart to decrease the blood flow and increase the patient’s ability to clot at the injured site.
  • If the direct pressure and elevation of the affected body part doesn’t aid in control of bleeding, then one should apply the indirect pressure to any of the pressure points situated along the main arteries. To apply the indirect pressure, the nurse will use two finger or the heel of her hand to compress the artery located between the heart and the wound. The most common pressure points are carotid, subclavian, brachial and femoral arteries.
  • Use of tourniquet is only indicated when the bleeding doesn’t control by these three step approach: Direct pressure - Elevation of the affected limb above the heart level - Indirect pressure.

choices.title: Urine output
choices.correct_explanation:
• Of all the options, urine output is the most reliable indicator for determining the adequacy of fluid resuscitation. Strict intake and output need to be monitored to rule out the fluid resuscitation. Indwelling Foley’s catheter can be inserted to monitor the I and O accurately.
  • Level of consciousness: While changes in level of consciousness can indicate fluid status or shock, it is a less direct and less specific indicator compared to urine output. Alterations in consciousness can result from various factors, not just fluid imbalance.
  • Peripheral pulses can provide information about circulation and perfusion. However, they can be affected by factors like vasoconstriction or the patient’s overall condition, making them less reliable as the sole indicator of fluid resuscitation adequacy.
  • Vital signs, including blood pressure and heart rate, are important to monitor and can indicate shock or hypovolemia. However, they are not as specific as urine output in assessing the effectiveness of fluid resuscitation, as vital signs can be influenced by many variables.

Note: Water in the water seal chamber fluctuates when the patient inhales and exhales. Water in the water seal chamber will increase during inspiration and decrease during expiration (it will be the opposite if the patient is on positive pressure mechanical ventilation). This process is called oscillation. Normal gentle continuous bubbling is normal finding where as excessive bubbling in the water seal chamber indicates an air leak.

  • Option a and c: The nurse should never clamp or milk/squeeze the chest tube catheter as it will create extreme negative pressure in the chest and can result into tension pneumothorax.

The priority nursing action in this case will be to check the insertion site for any kink or obstruction and should correct the cause.
